title: Rules, states, and win conditions in video games: a guide
summary: Learn how rules, game states, and win and lose conditions work in video games, with simple examples and a five-step method to define yours before you build.
body_markdown:
### What makes a good game goal?


Players should never have to ask whether they’ve won. If they do, the goal is probably too vague. A good goal is also attractive: the act of reaching it should sound enjoyable. And it should be exact, even if the ways of reaching it are flexible. If you start by[naming the feeling you want players to have](https://unity.com/blog/define-your-video-game) , check that your goal serves it.


Goals can work on three time scales:


- Short-term goals are bite-sized and give quick feedback.
- Mid-term goals take longer but fit within a session or a few sessions.
- Long-term goals give the whole game a direction.


Objectives are the stepping stones between them. Some are required, some are optional, and some are timed. Time pressure adds tension, so use it carefully unless it’s central to your core loop.


### Four questions to ask about every game ending


For each game, and each level, ask:


1. How can the player win?
2. How can the player lose?
3. Can the game end in a draw, or get stuck so that neither is possible?
4. What happens right after: what does the player see, and what can they do next?


The third question catches endings you didn’t plan for. In the grid example, you write the draw into the rules on purpose. An ending you didn’t plan for, like a level players can no longer finish, can leave players stuck with no way forward.


### How to keep players invested in your game


First, players disengage once they believe they can’t win. A catch-up feature, such as a swing in luck or a bonus for those who are behind, gives players something to hope for.


Second, a game should push toward its own ending. Length is a common problem in first designs, and a game should end before players want to stop. In a video game, that might mean difficulty ramps up, a timer runs, or each level has a[clear exit](https://unity.com/blog/level-design-basics) .
